# VERIFICATION.md — live-browser test checklist

Some changes pass every check we can run **without a browser** — `npm run lint`,
`npm test`, `npm run build`, and server-side endpoint calibration — but still need a
human (or a Claude coworker with a real browser) to confirm they actually work **in the
running app**. This file is the running list of those, so nothing that "builds green but
was never clicked" quietly ships broken.

> **Production app:** https://planyr.io (Cloudflare Pages, deploys from `main`).
> **This is the runtime counterpart to `BACKLOG.md`.** An item can be `[x]` done in the
> backlog and still ⏳ unverified here — the code landed; the click-through hasn't.

> ## ⚠️ Testing policy (updated 2026-06-17 — read this)
> **Michael does NOT click through to test things himself. Ever.** Don't wait on him, don't ask
> him to verify, don't end a turn expecting him to go look.
> **Claude self-verifies in a headless browser — in the same session, no separate "cohort."**
> A headless Chromium is available in the environment (see "🤖 Self-verification" below), so a
> session that ships a UI change should **drive the live app itself** and record the result rather
> than file the click-through for someone else. The working rhythm:
> - After a change is **CI-green + build-green**, **run the headless-browser check yourself**, then
>   record the outcome here (✅/❌ + date). Don't punt it.
> - **Only if no browser is reachable** (rare), log the item below and move on — never block on Michael.
> - **Do NOT surface "these N are unverified" to Michael as a to-do for him.**
> - **Only interrupt Michael for a genuinely CRITICAL problem** — the app won't build, won't render
>   (blank screen), or a shipped feature is visibly crashing in production. Everything else: note it
>   here, keep moving.
>
> ### 🤖 Self-verification — how (proven 2026-06-17 against planyr.io + per-branch preview URLs)
> Write a short Playwright script and run it with Node:
> - Browsers live at `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH=/opt/pw-browsers`; the module is the global
>   `/opt/node22/lib/node_modules/playwright` (require it by absolute path).
> - The sandbox egress proxy intercepts TLS, so launch with `args:['--ignore-certificate-errors']`
>   **and** `newContext({ ignoreHTTPSErrors: true })`, or `page.goto` throws `ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID`.
> - **Logged-out only:** that proxy also CORS-blocks the Supabase auth handshake, so self-tests run in
>   **this-device (logged-out) mode** — full coverage for the planner/drawing tools, but anything that
>   *requires* sign-in (cloud save/sync) still needs a signed-in check elsewhere.
> - Enter the planner via the map toolbar's **"Select parcels ▾"** caret → **"Start blank"** (NEW-1,
>   2026-08-29 — "Start blank" is no longer its own button; `getByTestId("map-start-blank-menu-btn")`
>   then `getByTestId("map-start-blank-menu-item")` is the reliable two-step click); drive the SVG
>   canvas with `page.mouse` (CDP mouse events fire React's pointer handlers); `page.screenshot({clip})`
>   then read the PNG back to eyeball it.

>
> ### 🚚 Confirming a change is actually SERVED (B1119) — use the script, not a hand grep
> `node ui-audit/verify-deploy.mjs <marker> [marker…]` (`--origin=` for a preview URL, `--json` for
> a machine-readable result). It walks the REAL module graph — index.html → entry chunk → every
> hashed chunk the entry names — and reports which chunk carries each marker, exiting non-zero if
> any is missing. **Do not hand-grep `assets/index-*.js`.** Two facts make that wrong here and it has
> already produced a confident false "never deployed" that cost a 2.5-hour deploy chase (2026-07-29):
> **(a)** Vite content-hashes every chunk SEPARATELY, so the entry's hash is UNCHANGED across a
> deploy whenever its own bytes didn't change — a stable index hash is evidence of nothing; and
> **(b)** almost all planner code lives in the LAZY `SitePlannerApp-*.js` chunk, so a string added to
> `lib/elementApi.js` was never going to appear in the entry at all.
> **Pick a MINIFY-SAFE marker** or you get the same false negative in a new costume: safe = a
> wire-level object key (`p_atomic`), user-visible copy, or a public-API property name; unsafe = any
> local function or variable name (`closeAssemblies` is renamed away by the build).
> **A green build check and the served bytes are DIFFERENT CLAIMS** — only ever report "deployed"
> off the bytes.

## How to use this — Claude Code / coworkers, read on every run

1. **Scan the 🔲 list below** — items waiting to be confirmed in the running app. Per the testing
   policy above, do **not** hand this list to Michael as his to-do; only escalate a **critical**
   (won't build / won't render / crashing) issue.
2. **Verify it yourself in a headless browser** (see "🤖 Self-verification" above): run the
   **Steps**, compare to **Expect**, then record the outcome.
3. **⛔ CLEAR OUT what you finish — don't leave passed items piling up here (owner rule, 2026-07-02).**
   This is the #1 reason this file bloats. Whoever runs a check (usually Claude Cowork on the live app —
   NOT Michael) archives it the SAME session, by item type:
   - **One-off item** (`Cadence: once` — a bug/feature acceptance check): once it **fully passes with
     nothing pending**, **MOVE its whole block to `docs/archive/VERIFICATION-DONE.md`** — do not just mark it ✅ and
     leave it here. (Same archiving discipline as `BACKLOG.md → docs/archive/BACKLOG-DONE.md`.) If it only *partly*
     passes (some steps still owed), it **stays** with the passed parts noted and the remainder ⏳.
   - **Recurring item** (`🌐` endpoint-liveness / any `Cadence: every N days`): it **stays here** —
     don't archive it. Just record the run: flip the status, set `Last checked`, bump `Next check` by
     the `Cadence`. These are meant to be re-run forever.
   - A **❌** stays ❌ (with the date + what broke) until it's re-fixed and re-run — never archive a fail.
4. **⛔ ATTEMPT before you PARK — a logged-out, no-external-GIS UI check is NEVER a valid "needs a live
   pass" item (owner rule, 2026-07-18, after too many Claude-doable checks were parked for a human).**
   Before you file OR leave a `V###` as pending, you must FIRST drive the headless self-verify. You may
   only defer an item if it hits one of exactly THREE hard walls — and it must NAME which, in a
   `Blocker:` field on the entry:
   - **`Blocker: auth`** — needs sign-in. The egress proxy CORS-blocks the Supabase auth handshake, so
     the sandbox genuinely cannot log in (a network-policy wall, not a missing password — a test login
     alone does not unlock it without a matching network-policy change).
   - **`Blocker: live-GIS`** — needs a live external map/GIS host the sandbox egress blocks (county
     flood / parcel / TxGIO services, etc.).
   - **`Blocker: real-data`** — needs a specific SIGNED-IN saved project (Tsakiris / Bain) that only
     exists in a real account.
   - **`Blocker: print-engine`** *(added 2026-07-31 with **V631**, and flagged rather than smuggled in:
     this is a FOURTH wall, and the rule above says three.)* — needs the browser's real PRINT pipeline.
     Headless Chromium's `window.print()` is a **no-op**: it produces no paginated output at all, so
     nothing in this sandbox can judge how a document breaks across sheets or what "Save as PDF"
     actually yields. The DOCUMENT we hand the browser is fully drivable here and **must** be driven
     (its content, its images, its styling, what chrome it drops) — only the step after our code is
     walled. Use this ONLY for that step; a print feature parked without its sheet having been driven
     is still a mis-classification.
   - **`Blocker: live-deploy`** *(added 2026-07-31 with **V669**, and flagged rather than smuggled in:
     this is a FIFTH wall.)* — needs a REAL deploy to land under an already-open tab. The sandbox can
     fabricate a newer build stamp and a route its build cannot resolve (and **must** — both halves of
     the mechanism are drivable here and are driven in `verify-notes.mjs` §21); what it cannot do is
     publish to Cloudflare Pages and watch a live tab notice. Use this ONLY for the step after our
     code: the edge's caching of the stamp file, and the reload landing on the new build.
   Everything else — draw / reshape / select / toggle / keyboard / export a blank site, the landing
   page, a dropped LOCAL file, a boot-recovery flow — is Claude-doable HERE: **drive it and record
   ✅/❌ this same session; do NOT park it.** A `V###` with no `Blocker:` wall is a mis-classification,
   not a to-do. (Still: never mark ✅ from reading code — confirming-in-the-running-app is the point.)
5. **Endpoint-liveness items (tagged 🌐) are the exception to "needs a browser"** — a `curl`/REST
   probe, runnable without a browser. Run those when due (and per rule 3 they stay, they don't archive).

`CLAUDE.md` points every session here, so this list is consulted automatically.

**Why this needs its own real pass.** Reaching this state requires a real parcel click against live county GIS parcel data (a mandatory GIS-endpoint-behavior LIVE-VERIFY class) — the sandbox's headless crawl can arm Comp mode and select-mode by a plain click, but cannot click an actual parcel polygon on the map without live GIS data resolving under it.

**What was verified here.** The `NESTED_ACTION_SIZE` conversion was applied to this exact code (`MapFinder.jsx`'s "Plan {N} parcels →" / "Comp {N} parcels" buttons, both `mode === "site"` and `mode === "comp"` branches) in the same edit as the buttons `ui-audit/ui-inventory.mjs` could reach (Drop a pin / Comp from parcel / both Cancel buttons) — confirmed by direct source read, not left unmeasured. `npx vitest run` is green (668/668 files) and `node ui-audit/locked-primitive-audit.mjs --check` / `node ui-audit/design-drift-audit.mjs --check` both pass on the changed file. What could NOT be confirmed here is the RENDERED result — whether the live browser actually paints these two buttons at the intended `(radius:6, height:30, padding:"0 12px", fontSize:12)` tuple once a real selection exists.

**Steps, each with a named expected result — on `planyr.io`, either theme:**
1. Open the map landing page (no project open) → click "＋ Select parcels" → click a real parcel on the map. **Expect:** the search bar's right section shows a small orange status dot, "1 parcel · N.NN AC", a small ✕ clear button, and a filled "Plan site →" button.
2. Click a second, adjoining parcel. **Expect:** the label updates to "2 parcels · N.NN AC" and the button relabels to "Plan 2 parcels →".
3. Measure "Plan site →" against "Drop a pin"/"Comp from parcel" (switch to Comp mode, select a parcel there to compare against "Comp N parcels"). **Expect:** all of them read as the same height and corner rounding as each other and as "Select parcels ▾" — no visible size jump when the row's content changes from the resting state to the post-selection state.

**Result:** ⏳ pending — needs a real parcel click against live county GIS data; not reachable from this sandbox's logged-out headless crawl.

### V556720 — B986096: paste Michael's exact lease abstract into the Comps entry card stack, confirm one card / full field coverage / labelled layout, save, and read the row back from `public.comps` `Blocker: auth`

**Why this needs its own real pass.** The parse→render→save round trip is client-side parsing feeding a real signed-in Supabase write; a saved row and its stored values, plus the actual click-through (the "one record, three rows" bug's fix, the location picker over the live map, the quick-resolve buttons), can only be confirmed against the live database and a real signed-in browser session.

**History — FOUR owner-measured hardening rounds, all fixed and re-verified this session (do not re-diagnose any of these):**
1. **Shape detection.** The original spec ("one pasted line = one row") was wrong for the dominant real shape — Michael's own 10-line lease abstract produced 32 junk "Land" rows. Fixed with `detectPasteShape` (spreadsheet → labeled-single-record → completeness-based single/multi default).
2. **Five owner-measured live-bundle bugs**: a full-viewport modal backdrop physically blocked the map buttons it told the user to click; typing didn't parse; the shape-detection bug was still live; the paste box cleared itself; lease-row layout was broken in the shared-column grid.
3. **Field coverage.** A column-by-column audit of `public.comps` against the form found `title` reachable NOWHERE in the UI — a real regression from the pre-rebuild single-comp form.
4. **THE CONTAINER ITSELF WAS WRONG, owner's own words: "I specified a shared-column grid... every lease row has to cram twelve fields into columns sized for four."** The shared-column row grid is GONE, replaced with one CARD per comp laid out for its own type (full spec on the B986096 backlog item). ALSO fixed this round: the "one record, three rows" bug — the banner said "Treated as ONE record" while the footer showed 3 rows, 2 nearly empty. Root cause: Pass 2's "parse on any embedded newline in onChange" heuristic could fire more than once for what the user experienced as one paste. Eliminated (not patched): `onChange` is now a plain state update; the only two commit paths are a real clipboard paste and an explicit Add/Ctrl+Enter action, plus a duplicate-text dedupe guard. **This mechanism could not be reproduced in this sandbox (no live browser) — the fix is a structural elimination of the one fragile mechanism capable of producing the symptom, verified by code trace, not a recording. This is exactly what step 2 below has to confirm.**

**What was verified here (this pass, without a browser).** Ran Michael's **exact** 10-line paste through the real, unmocked production pipeline (`parsePaste` → `emptyDraft`/`draftToComp`/`compToRow`) — **10/10 facts land in the right column**, including the new source-quoted commencement note: `Date read from "Commencement estimated to be June 1, 2027" — stored as estimated, not as a signing date.` Then a REAL write against production `public.comps` (project `lyeqzkuiwngunutlkkmi`) via the Supabase MCP: inserted that exact row under the owner's own account, read it back with a fresh, separate `SELECT` (proving real persistence, not an insert echo), confirmed every field byte-for-byte (`lease_size_sf: "613208"`, `lease_escalation_pct: "3.5"`, `title: "20320 West Hardy Road - Building A"`), then deleted the test row — no residue left on the owner's account. Full `npx vitest run` green (38 comps-parse tests, 3 new this round). `npm run build` / `npx eslint` / `node ui-audit/design-drift-audit.mjs --check` / `node scripts/build-map.mjs --check` / `node ui-audit/doc-pointer-audit.mjs` all clean.
**Attempted again this pass and still could NOT complete — same wall as before, re-confirmed, not re-diagnosed:** a headless Chromium request to `https://planyr.io/?cb=<ts>` failed with `net::ERR_CONNECTION_RESET` from this session's sandboxed proxy (matching every prior session's finding; already ruled out as planyr.io-specific via a control test against unrelated hosts). Per `CLAUDE.md`'s documented split, a Claude Code session cannot sign in here — the actual click-through needs a session that CAN drive a real signed-in browser (the Cowork thread, per `verification-inbox/`) or Michael's own pass.

### V474576 — B853266 + B853267: the project registry backfill/reconcile fixes a real project missing from the switcher — and its own search finding it — on the owner's actual diverged account `Blocker: auth` `Blocker: real-data`
**UPDATE 2026-08-30 — LIVE PASS RUN. CONFIRMED PASS on four of five surfaces; the fifth (Schedule) found FAILING, root cause found, and fixed this same session.** Owner drove all four routes on planyr.io directly: **Site** (`/project/<id>/site`, hard reload, first dropdown open) — Richfield at top marked "current", then Richey 3h/Woods Road 23h/Bain 1d/Grand Port 1d/Goose Creek 1d/JFK 3d/Hoffmeister 3d/Schiel 3d, plus a collapsed "Recently deleted, 11" section; typing "Silv" finds Silvestri 4d. **Library, Review, Notes** — same list, same current marker, same timestamps, confirmed correct. **Schedule** (both `/project/<id>/schedule` and the global `/schedule` dashboard, hard reload, first dropdown open each, ~1 minute apart, throttle not in play) — showed only the OLD static six (Goose Creek, Grand Port, 8 South, Pursuits, Pappadoupolos, Operations) with no current marker, no timestamps, no bin. Root cause: Scheduler is the only caller that renders the breadcrumb in "controlled" mode (its own `projects=` prop bridges the embedded Gantt app's schedule list, a structurally different list from the site registry), and controlled mode's `if (controlled) return;` guards skipped the whole registry data layer this fix built — not a duplicated header, the same shared component reading a different data shape. Fixed via `unionProjectLists()` (new pure helper) + un-gating the data layer from `controlled` — see B853266's own updated backlog note for the full mechanism. Unit-tested in `test/projects.test.js`. `npm test` full suite green, lint 0 errors, build green, bundle budget within band.
**What was verified originally, without a real signed-in pass.** The root cause (a local site-list cache that only self-heals when totally EMPTY, never when merely diverged from the cloud) is traced to exact lines in `shared/projects/projects.js` and `ProjectBreadcrumb.jsx` by an Explore agent, and confirmed against that module's own header comments, which already documented the class of bug ("a device that went straight to another workspace... the switcher looked empty right next to surfaces that query Supabase live") without ever closing the non-empty-but-stale case. The fix — `reconcileProjects()` (always-pull, throttled, fired on dropdown open) + `withCurrentProject()` (synchronous backfill of the routed project) — is unit-tested in `test/projects.test.js`: backfill when missing, untouched-identity (`toBe`) when already present, the "Untitled site" fallback, a no-op with no current project, and — directly matching B853267's reported repro — that `filterProjects` finds the backfilled current project by its own name.
**What is STILL NOT proven, and cannot be from this sandbox.** Schedule's own fix (`unionProjectLists`) is unit-tested at the pure-function level and confirmed to build/lint/test clean, but nobody has watched it render correctly on the owner's real, signed-in, diverged Schedule route yet — that is the one remaining live step.
**Steps, each with a named expected result:**
1. ✅ DONE 2026-08-30 — Site, Library, Review, Notes: current-project marker, timestamps, search, and the recently-deleted bin all confirmed correct live.
2. On `planyr.io`, signed in, open the same project's Schedule tab (`/project/<id>/schedule`), hard reload, open the project switcher. **Expect:** the SAME full list Site/Library/Review/Notes show — real projects with timestamps, the current project marked, the recently-deleted bin present — union'd with any schedule-only pseudo-projects (Pursuits/Operations) that have no site id.
3. Repeat step 2 on the global `/schedule` dashboard (no project routed). **Expect:** the same union'd list; no current marker (nothing is routed).
4. Pick a real project (e.g. Richfield) from the Schedule switcher. **Expect:** it navigates to that project's schedule (or offers to link/create one) exactly as picking it from any other route's switcher would — no crash, no dead click.

### V463840 — B842528: markers no longer draw at wrong positions during a real zoom, on the owner's own account and hardware `Blocker: auth` `Blocker: real-data`
**What was verified here, extensively, without a real device pass.** The root cause is proven by direct citation of Leaflet's own vendored source (`node_modules/leaflet/dist/leaflet-src.js`): `Canvas.prototype._updatePath` unconditionally calls `layer._project()` before repainting, and `Renderer.prototype._onAnimZoom` re-applies the ambient CSS transform on every `'zoomanim'` frame from the renderer's own last-settled zoom — a genuine double transform when both fire in the same gesture, which the removed per-frame `setRadius` compensation loop caused every frame. This was then MEASURED, not just reasoned about: `.scratch-repro/verify-marker-position.mjs`, real headless Chromium, real Leaflet, the real `FoodMap` component, synthetic markers at the owner's own real Austin-area cluster (queried live against production) plus Dallas/San Antonio test points at different distances from Houston. Mid-animation deltas of 100–300px+ on the pre-fix code (both via the +/- zoom buttons and a real multi-touch pinch simulated through raw CDP), with the farther test point consistently showing a larger error — the exact distance signature the owner's own hypothesis predicted. After the fix (the whole per-frame mechanism removed), the same gestures show 0 `setRadius` calls during animation and resting deltas of 0.7px. A permanent regression guard (`ui-audit/verify-marker-position.mjs`) codifies both checks and passes.
**What is NOT proven, and why it parks here.** Nobody has pinched-to-zoom on the owner's own phone, on his own real (not synthetic) Austin/Houston data, and confirmed the fix feels right there — the synthetic test points, while placed at his real coordinates, are not his actual 145+ real places, and a real device's touch/rendering pipeline could behave subtly differently from a CDP-simulated pinch.
**Steps, each with a named expected result:**
1. Sign in on `planyr.io`, open a place he's logged near Austin, and pinch-zoom out on a real phone to a whole-Texas view. **Expect:** his eleven real Austin-area visits collapse into a single dot sitting ON Austin — never a marker drifting southeast toward Houston or anywhere else with no real place.
2. Pinch back in. **Expect:** the cluster separates back into individual, correctly-placed pins with no lingering displacement.
3. Repeat both directions using the +/- zoom control buttons on desktop. **Expect:** same — no displacement in either direction.
4. After any zoom gesture settles, tap a pin near where several places are close together. **Expect:** it opens the CORRECT place's detail panel — confirms hit-testing agrees with drawing, not just that the picture looks right.
**Result:** ⏳ pending — needs a real-device pinch-zoom pass on planyr.io with the owner's own real data; the root cause, the measured before/after pixel deltas, the fix, and a permanent structural regression guard are all proven live above against synthetic data at his real coordinates.

Confirmed: opening edit via a card tap AND via the `···` menu's new Edit item both work; every field pre-fills exactly from the visit's current values (rating, date, "what I had", cost, all correctly coerced); Cancel writes nothing (0 calls to the edit callback) and restores the original card; a successful Save updates the card in place with the new value; a forced failure keeps the form open with the typed value intact and shows a real error, never silently discarding it; Cancelling out of a failed edit shows the last REAL saved value, never the failed, never-written attempt. `updateVisit` (the real Supabase call) is confirmed to be a plain, unbypassed PostgREST `.update()`, which fires the `food_visits_touch_updated_at` DB trigger (confirmed present in `db/food.sql`) — the attribution mechanism for this edit.
**What is NOT proven, and why it parks here.** Nobody has actually edited a real visit on the owner's own signed-in `planyr.io` account against the real Supabase backend — that's the only way to confirm the real network round-trip, real latency, and the DB trigger firing on a genuine production write (as opposed to the harness's fake, instant-resolving callback), and that the map pin (not exercised by the panel-only harness) visibly updates if an edited rating changes a place's average.
**Steps, each with a named expected result:**
1. Sign in on `planyr.io`, open a place with a past visit, and tap the visit card. **Expect:** it opens inline as an editable form with every field showing its real current value.
2. Change the rating and save. **Expect:** the card shows the new value immediately, the score-strip aggregates above it recompute, and the map pin updates if this changes the place's average rating.
3. Reload the page (or re-open the place). **Expect:** the edited value persists — confirms the write actually reached the database, not just local state.
4. Edit a visit again, this time via the `···` menu's Edit item, change a value, then press Cancel. **Expect:** the card still shows the value from step 2 — nothing from the cancelled edit was written.
5. Force a failure (e.g. go offline) and try to save an edit. **Expect:** a real error shows, the form stays open with the typed value, and reloading confirms nothing changed in the database.
**Result:** ⏳ pending — needs a real signed-in pass on planyr.io to confirm the full write-then-read-back against real Supabase data; the form reuse, pre-fill, optimistic update, rollback-on-failure, and the DB-enforced attribution timestamp are all measured live above against the real, unmodified components.

### V445488 — B800848: the Contour lines layer no longer lags a real signed-in plan while panning/zooming `Blocker: live-GIS`
**What was verified here, extensively, without a live 3DEP round-trip completing.** This sandbox's Chromium cannot reach `elevation.nationalmap.gov` at all (`net::ERR_CONNECTION_RESET`, confirmed again this session — Node's own `fetch` reaches it, Playwright's Chromium does not), so no contour line has ever been paintable here through the real network path. To still measure something real rather than reason about it, `ui-audit/diagnose-contour-pan-perf.mjs` (new) intercepts every `exportImage` request and answers with the REAL captured LERC tile `test/fixtures/dep-katy-463x400.lerc`, which let contours actually render, repaint and be paced through a genuine pan sequence in a headless build for the first time. Two builds were compared — a `dist-before` from the pre-fix source and the fixed `dist` — driving an identical, real, continuous 14-step pan (never revisiting ground) at working zoom 18, with the per-step ground shift calibrated from the lattice tile's own real span rather than guessed in screen pixels. Measured via CDP `Performance.getMetrics`: **106.3 ms → 102.6 ms median main-thread work per pan step (−3.5%)**. Separately, and more rigorously, the exact mechanism the fix depends on was proven against the same real captured tile in Node-level unit tests (`test/terrainLattice.test.js`): repainting an identical view is a total no-op for the new diff (zero Leaflet objects added or removed), and dropping one tile from the cover (simulating it panning out of view) retires only the geometry that actually touched it while an untouched tile's own contours keep their identity and are never rebuilt.
**What is NOT proven, and why it parks here.** Nobody has opened a real, signed-in (or logged-out) plan on `planyr.io`, turned on "Contour lines (1 ft)" at a working zoom, and panned/zoomed around to confirm it *feels* less laggy — that needs the real 3DEP service, which this sandbox cannot reach. The measured −3.5% end-to-end improvement is honest but smaller than the owner's report would suggest is needed; profiling why turned up a SEPARATE, larger cost (`composeContourPaint`'s full per-level recomposition, ~24 ms/repaint, unrelated to this fix) that is filed as its own follow-up (**B800849**) rather than rushed into this same change. A possible redundant tile-refetch pattern was also observed and filed, honestly, as unconfirmed (**B800850**) — it may be a defect, or it may be an artifact of this session's specific test harness; either way it needs a real network path to settle.
**Steps, each with a named expected result:**
1. On `planyr.io` (signed in or out), open or start a plan near a real US location with 3DEP LiDAR coverage (most of the continental US). Zoom in to site/neighborhood scale (roughly the zoom you'd draw buildings at). **Expect:** the Layers panel is reachable and "Contour lines (1 ft)" is listed under GIS layers.
2. Turn on "Contour lines (1 ft)". **Expect:** after a brief load, thin brown 1-ft contour lines appear, with heavier lines and elevation labels every 5 ft — no change in appearance or precision from before this fix.
3. Pan around continuously (drag the map) for 10–15 seconds, covering new ground rather than panning back and forth over the same spot. **Expect:** noticeably less stutter/freeze than before — the owner's originally reported lag should be reduced. (It may not be eliminated — see the honest caveat above; if it still lags badly, that's evidence for B800849/B800850, not a regression in this fix.)
4. Zoom in and out a few times with contours on. **Expect:** same as step 3 — smoother than the pre-fix build, not necessarily perfect.
5. Compare a "before" feel if possible (the previous deployed build, or ask whether it felt different before this shipped). **Expect:** an improvement is perceptible, even if modest.
**Result:** ⏳ pending — needs a real 3DEP round-trip on `planyr.io`, which this sandbox's blocked GIS egress cannot complete; the fix is proven correct and effective in isolation (real captured DEM data, Node-level unit tests) and shows a real, measured, honestly-modest improvement in a full before/after browser comparison against two real builds. `Blocker: live-GIS`

**What was verified here, extensively, without a browser download completing.** The root cause (an unconverted 7-screen-px legibility floor on the callout arrowhead, and a constant-canvas-px hatch tile with no export correction) was proven mathematically and reproduced exactly: measured on a real capture at `rppf=0.023058736`, the pre-fix arrowhead baked a **303.6 ft** world size where the design intends **26.0 ft** (11.7× oversize), and the hatch tile baked the same 303.6 ft footprint regardless of the framed area. Beyond the SVG-structure math, the actual PICTURE was checked: the export clone was rasterized through a byte-faithful replica of `restyleExportClone`'s full stroke-thinning pass (attribute width, inline-style width, and the dash-array rescale — copied from the real source, not approximated) at both a normal editing zoom and a 20-notch-out wide zoom, for both a callout+building scene and an easement+parcel scene. So nobody has actually clicked Download PDF, opened the resulting file in a real PDF viewer, and looked at it — the rasterization replica above is the closest a sandbox without that network path can get, and it is a faithful reproduction of the real rendering mechanism (genuine browser SVG-to-canvas rasterization, the same `<img>`+`drawImage` approach `exportPDF` itself uses), not a simulation of it.
**Steps, each with a named expected result:**

### V425920 — B768160: OCR a scanned deed PDF into a correctly-plottable legal description, on the owner's real scanned deed
**What was verified here — the whole pipeline (render → preprocess → Tesseract → repair/reflow → deedParse.js → closure) driven end to end in headless Chromium against the REAL shipped code, twice, at two degradation levels, plus the owner's own independent real-deed measurement.** `ui-audit/verify-ocr-scanned-deed.mjs` renders a legal description (the same construct set as the owner's real deed: a curve with radius/central-angle/arc/chord, a passing-at/total-distance clause, a parenthetical offset note) to a canvas, degrades it the way a repeated photocopy scan degrades (skew, noise, dropped contrast, a resample-down-and-up blur), builds a real text-less PDF from it (pdf-lib), and feeds that PDF straight into `ocrScannedDeedPdf` — the exact function `readDeeds`/`ocrScannedPdfInto` call in `SitePlanner.jsx`.
- **Realistic photocopy-scan degradation** (skew 1.6°, mild noise, moderate contrast loss, resample blur): mean OCR confidence 94.1%. **6/6 courses found, 6/6 bearings correct (azimuth within 0.5°, distance within 1% or 0.5 ft), traverse CLOSES at 0.60 ft misclosure** — effectively exact, and closure error alone would never have raised a flag. Wall clock 43s for one page.
- **Harsher stress degradation** (skew 2.4°, heavier noise, contrast dropped further, heavier resample blur): mean OCR confidence still a plausible-looking 85.1%, but **0/6 bearings recovered exactly** — digit-level corruption (0→6/8, dropped/altered characters) got past the repair rules. **The closure safety net did exactly its job: misclosure 894 ft on a ~2,500 ft traverse — unmissable, not a silently-plausible wrong polygon.** This is the case CLAUDE.md item (f) exists for: a bad OCR read produces a LOUD, obvious "does NOT close" warning (with the low-confidence/suspect-distance culprit calls named in the UI), never a quiet wrong boundary.
- **The owner's own independent measurement, on his real recorded deed (Chambers County, "16 - Recorded Correction SWD.pdf," a 1-bit CCITT-G4 scan, no preprocessing, stock Tesseract):** 19/19 bearings recovered, exactly ONE true character error (a doubled degree sign standing in for a minutes prime — this session added a targeted, unit-tested repair for exactly that pattern) plus two harmless word slips ("arc"→"are", "to a"→"toa" — also repaired). His real scan is CLEANER than either synthetic case above, which is the expected shape for a direct scan of a stamped recorded instrument (vs. this fixture's simulated repeated-photocopy degradation).
- **A real, unrelated bug found and fixed along the way (the owner's own item (3) audit ask):** the construct-coverage fixture (`test/deedRealDeedAudit.test.js`) proved `deedParse.js` — the SAME parser every non-OCR path already uses — correctly handles curves, passing-at/total-distance, offset notes, tie calls, and SAVE AND EXCEPT tracts, closing to sub-foot tolerance; a SAVE AND EXCEPT tract's LABEL (cosmetic only) was picking up the wrong acreage figure and was fixed.
- **A real defect this session found in ITS OWN first draft, worth recording so it isn't rediscovered:** the first OCR pass fed Tesseract's raw multi-line text straight to `deedParse.js` and a wrapped curve clause silently split into unparseable fragments (0/6 recovered, misclosure 1,270 ft) — NOT an OCR quality problem, a missing reflow step (the same wrapped-line rejoin `pdfText.js` already does for a text-layer PDF, extracted to `deedTextReflow.js` and reused). Fixed and reverified before this V### was written; left here as the concrete instance of "don't blame OCR for a parsing gap" the owner asked to guard against.
**What is NOT proven here.** The owner's actual PDF was not available to this session (he described it; the file itself isn't attached) — this is the closest a sandbox can get without it. Signed-in behavior (does the OCR'd + user-edited text survive a save/reload like any other deed queue row) rides the SAME `deedQueue`/`mbText` state every other deed-file path already uses and wasn't re-tested separately. The page-picker UI (for a 20-page boilerplate-heavy deed) and the low-confidence highlight overlay were unit- and component-level tested but not eyeballed in a real signed-in click-through.
- Blocker: real-data — closing this fully needs either the owner's actual PDF or a live click-through on planyr.io with a real scanned deed.
**Steps, each with a named expected result:**
1. Open the Title reader & metes-and-bounds plotter, drop a scanned (no text layer) deed PDF. **Expect:** instead of "This PDF looks scanned…", a quiet progress row appears ("Reading scanned PDF with OCR — page 1 of N… Recognizing text… NN%") with a Cancel button.
2. Wait for it to finish. **Expect:** the paste box fills with the read text; any low-confidence word is highlighted (a soft amber background); a multi-page deed additionally shows a page picker ("All N pages" / "Page 1" / "Page 2" / …) so a specific page can be loaded instead of the concatenation.
3. Click "Plot on canvas" without editing anything. **Expect:** if the calls close, it plots normally; if they don't, the existing "these calls don't close" warning ALSO names the specific call(s) most likely at fault ("Likely OCR culprit — check call 3 (…) — NN% OCR confidence").
4. Cancel mid-read on a multi-page scan. **Expect:** the progress row disappears, a toast reports how many pages were read before cancelling, and whatever text came from those pages is still usable.

**What was verified here — the false disabled-reason confirmed gone, endpoint deletion confirmed correct, the whole-element-delete offer confirmed at the true floor, all headless, real built app.** `ui-audit/verify-endpoint-delete.mjs` drives the real app logged out and passes **12/12**: drew a 3-point road (start/turn/end — the owner's exact repro shape), right-clicked the START endpoint, and confirmed "Delete control point" reads ENABLED (not "min reached"); clicked it and confirmed the road shortens to 2 points with the surviving vertex's feet-coordinates proven identical to the old middle "turn" point (the CAD/GIS "shorten the line" behavior). On the resulting 2-point road, right-clicked the remaining endpoint and confirmed the menu now offers "Delete road" (the dead disabled row is gone); clicked it and confirmed the road is removed entirely. Repeated end-to-end for a freshly-drawn 2-point centerline EASEMENT ("Delete easement" offered and works) and a 2-point Length MEASUREMENT, which is always exactly 2 points ("Delete measurement" offered and works).
**The audit side, also verified by direct code reading (not just behavior):** every other vertex-edited element type (parcels, buildings/paving/sidewalk/parking/pond, markups, easement boundaries) already computed deletability generically (`pts.length > min`) with no endpoint singled out — only the road layer had the exclusion, so no other element type needed a code change; this was confirmed by reading every `deleteVtx`/`editablePath` branch, not assumed. Three panel hint strings (easement panel, generic markup panel, pond inspector) claimed a "Shift-click removes a point" gesture that measurably does not exist anywhere in the app (Shift-click only adds, on an edge) — corrected to state the true mechanism.
**What is NOT proven here.** This sandbox runs logged out, so cloud-saved-plan persistence of a shortened road (does the change survive a reload / sync to another tab) was not exercised — only local in-session state. The three corrected hint strings were verified to render the new (correct) text but not eyeballed for wrapping/legibility on the owner's real screen size.
**Steps, each with a named expected result:**

### V408192 — B742369: at real browser page zoom (Ctrl+/Ctrl−), a footprint corner drag still tracks the cursor 1:1
**What was verified here — the pointer→world transform audited and found to carry no zoom/devicePixelRatio term, and the DAMAGE this class of bug can do closed and proven regardless of the answer.** `p2f`/`screenToWorld` (`shared/viewport/viewportTransform.js`) is `world = (screen − t) / scale`, fed only by `MouseEvent.clientX/clientY` and `Element.getBoundingClientRect()` — both defined by the CSSOM View spec in the same "visual CSS pixel" space at any zoom level, so a uniform page zoom scales both together and their difference is invariant by construction; a repo-wide search of the drag path found no `devicePixelRatio`/`movementX`/`movementY` reference anywhere in it. Separately, and independent of that question: the self-crossing/degenerate guard that used to run only at pointer-up now runs on every drag frame, so an oversized pointer delta — whatever its cause — can no longer write an invalid polygon to state at all; it holds the vertex at the last valid position and warns. That half is proven live, headless, this session (`ui-audit/verify-b872-round2.mjs`, 4/4 checks).
**What is NOT proven, and why it parks here rather than closing on the audit alone:** whether the specific production observation — a corner drag overshooting ~5× at ~160% browser zoom — was actually CAUSED by zoom, or by something else that happened to coincide with it. This sandbox cannot drive Chrome's real Ctrl+/Ctrl− page zoom, which changes `window.devicePixelRatio` proportionally; the one proxy tried (`document.body.style.zoom`) was confirmed NOT equivalent — it changes `getBoundingClientRect()` numbers but leaves `devicePixelRatio` and `visualViewport.scale` at 1, unlike real page zoom. So the audit is strong evidence against zoom being the cause, not a live-machine proof.
**Steps, each with a named expected result:**
1. On a real machine (not this sandbox), open any plan and set the browser's page zoom (Ctrl+ / Ctrl− on Windows/Linux, ⌘+ / ⌘− on Mac) to roughly 150–175%. **Expect:** the app still renders and is usable at this zoom (a baseline sanity check, not the point of the test).
2. Select a building, "✎ Edit footprint (reshape)" (or via the right-click menu), and drag one corner a modest, ordinary distance — a few inches of mouse travel, nothing extreme. **Expect:** the corner tracks the cursor 1:1, the same feel as at 100% zoom — NOT a multi-times overshoot.
3. Repeat step 2 at 100% zoom on the same building for a direct comparison. **Expect:** identical tracking behavior between the two zoom levels.
4. If step 2 DOES still overshoot: note the exact zoom %, OS, browser, and whether a HiDPI/Retina display is involved, and file a fresh, narrower repro — but confirm first that the corner still refuses to cross the outline and holds with a "⚠ Reshape held…" toast rather than corrupting the saved plan (the fix this item shipped). A live failure of step 2 downgrades this from a data-integrity bug back to an input-tracking one; it does not reopen the data-integrity question, which the frame-by-frame guard closes independent of root cause.
**Result:** ⏳ pending — needs a real machine with real browser page zoom, which this sandbox cannot faithfully emulate.

### V400352 — B734529: "Find my location" recovers cleanly (never a permanent spinner) on the owner's REAL company-policy Chrome `Blocker: real-data`
**⛔ CORRECTED same day, by the owner's own measurement — read this before the rest.** This item originally asked to confirm `navigator.permissions.query({name:'geolocation'})` resolves `'denied'` on the owner's real Chrome. He measured it directly against the real deployed app: **it resolves `'prompt'`**, not `'denied'` — his company's policy blocks the geolocation request itself, silently, without pre-announcing through the Permissions API. So the steps below no longer ask him to look for a permanently-dimmed, pre-blocked icon (that would never have matched his environment); they ask him to confirm the ACTUAL defence — an explicit 10s timeout on the request plus an independent 12s watchdog, both proven in sandbox with `permissions.query` genuinely left un-mocked (reporting the real `'prompt'`) and `getCurrentPosition` mocked to never call back either way.
**What was verified here — every failure case, mocked but exact, against the real built control.** `test/locateMe.test.js` (27) pins the pure decisions: `isAccuracyUsable`/`ACCURACY_USABLE_THRESHOLD_M` (15 km ceiling, distinct from the existing 500 m tight-circle threshold), `locateAvailability` (insecure > unsupported > blocked > ready, checked in that priority order — 'prompt' correctly falls through to 'ready', matching the owner's real state), and `locateUnavailableTooltip` (a non-empty, distinct sentence for every state). `ui-audit/verify-locate-me.mjs` drives the REAL built app in headless Chromium and passes **30/30**: a mocked GENUINE-denial `navigator.permissions.query` (a real per-site browser block, a different case from the owner's) marks the control muted and a click on it neither spins nor calls `getCurrentPosition`; a live permission `change` event re-enables it; a mocked 50 km fix shows an honest "not accurate enough" failure and draws nothing; an unanswered prompt (mocked `getCurrentPosition` that never calls back) is proven to stop the spinner via the watchdog; **"THE CORRECTED SCENARIO" arm specifically leaves `permissions.query` real and un-mocked — it independently confirms Chromium here also reports `'prompt'` by default, matching the owner's measurement — then mocks only `getCurrentPosition` to call back neither way, and proves the control ends idle (not spinning), shows an honest message, and a fresh click successfully retries**; a 2nd click while a fix is in flight cancels immediately and a stale late resolution never revives the UI; aria-label/tooltip always present.
**What is NOT proven here.** Whether the owner's real geolocation provider, under his actual policy, behaves exactly like the mock (invoking neither callback) or produces some other shape (e.g. an eventual but slow error) — either way the explicit timeout + watchdog should recover cleanly, but that is the one thing only his own click can confirm. Also unconfirmed: that the honest message and the dimmed/blocked styling (for the DIFFERENT, genuine-'denied' case — e.g. if he later sets an explicit browser-level site block) read correctly to him visually, in both themes.
**Steps, each with a named expected result:**
1. On the owner's real work laptop (the one with the location-blocking policy), open `planyr.io/#/map` in Chrome (signed in or out — this control needs no sign-in). Find the small crosshair/target icon at the bottom-left of the map, directly below the +/− zoom buttons. **Expect:** it looks the SAME as the zoom buttons beside it (full strength, not dimmed) — his policy shape does not pre-announce, so the control correctly does not know ahead of time that it's blocked.
2. Click it. **Expect:** it spins briefly (this is expected and correct — the app cannot know in advance that this request is doomed), then — well within about 10-12 seconds — the spin stops on its own, the map does not move, and a short one-line note appears near the bottom-left of the map reading something like "Finding your location took too long — try again, or move somewhere with a clearer signal." **The one thing this step exists to catch: the spin must NOT continue past ~12 seconds, and it must NOT stay silent with no message.**
3. Click it again, right after step 2's message appears. **Expect:** it spins again (a fresh attempt, not stuck from before) and resolves the same honest way within the same ~10-12 seconds — proving the control isn't left in a stuck/dead state after the first failure.
4. If IT ever lifts the location-services block for this machine (or the owner tests on a different, unrestricted computer/phone instead): reload the map and click the icon. **Expect:** it spins briefly, then either centers the map on the real location or (indoors/no GPS/weak signal) shows the existing honest "approximate" message — never a permanent spinner, never longer than ~12 seconds either way.
5. On an unrestricted device with a real GPS/Wi-Fi fix, click the icon twice quickly. **Expect:** the second click either does nothing extra (if the first already finished) or visibly stops the first attempt (spinner stops) rather than the icon spinning indefinitely or the map jumping twice.
**Result:** ⏳ pending — needs the owner's own click-through on his real, policy-blocked Chrome to confirm the ~12-second recovery reads correctly (the mechanism is proven in sandbox against his own measured permission state; what's left is watching it happen).

**What was verified here — the mechanism, not the live symptom, across all four bugs in this item's history.** The sandbox's egress proxy blocks the real CARTO/Esri tile hosts this needs outright (`curl` to `a.basemaps.cartocdn.com:443` → `403`, gateway policy denial), so none of the four symptoms can be reproduced or re-confirmed here against real tile servers. ### V326384 — B851 (×2): the schedule grid no longer diverges from the route, and the false "newer version" reload banner stops firing from browsing projects `Blocker: real-data` `Blocker: auth`
**What was verified here — root cause reproduced by simulation, fix mutation-proven, not just plausible.** The recurrence (route "Goose Creek", grid showing Grand Port's tasks, plus a false "a newer version was saved on another device" reload prompt) traces to `public/sequence/index.html`'s `window.storage.set()` having no serialization: every `data` change fires an un-debounced `attemptCloudSave`, and the Scheduler's carry-in effect posts a real project-switch into the always-kept-alive Scheduler iframe on every app-wide routed-project change (even while Schedule isn't the visible tab, by design — B1342). Browsing a few Site Planner projects before landing on Schedule can put two or more real saves to `hs-v1` in flight at once; the optimistic-concurrency guard (`cloudRev > knownRev[k]`) is a plain read-then-write check with no server-side compare-and-swap, so overlapping same-tab saves that complete OUT OF ORDER let the LAST one to finish win outright, even when it was issued first and is now stale — with no conflict ever detected. A forced-ordering simulation using the REAL Layer-0 guard logic and the real `mergeCloudDoc` (the verbatim mirror already in `ui-audit/stress/scheduler-engine.mjs`) reproduced this: 2 of 3 realistic network-timing interleavings silently clobbered the correct value. The fix serializes `window.storage.set()` per key (coalescing adjacent AUTO saves, never coalescing an explicit checkpoint save); the same simulation converges correctly in all 3 interleavings after the fix. `test/schedulerSaveQueue.test.js` (8 tests, new) extracts the real queue wrapper from the shipped file (drift-proof) and proves both the pre-fix reproduction and the post-fix convergence. Full suite 12,020 green, lint 0 errors, build green, the Scheduler syntax guard (`ui-audit/stress/check-babel.mjs`) OK.
**What is NOT verified here, and why it needs his real account.** This is a timing-dependent race against his real ~338 KB `hs-v1` document under his actual multi-project browsing pattern — the sandbox's egress-blocked, signed-out environment can't drive the real embedded Scheduler at all (the same limitation every prior Scheduler nav-bridge item in this file notes), and the race by its nature won't force itself on demand in a live click-through either; the meaningful confirmation is the ABSENCE of the recurrence over normal use, not a single successful click.
**Steps, each with a named expected result:**
1. Signed in, browse several different Site Planner projects in quick succession (clicking through 3-4 project cards or breadcrumb entries within a few seconds), then open the Schedule tab on the last one. **Expect:** the grid shows that project's tasks; if it briefly shows a different project's tasks during the ~1s load window that's the ordinary self-healing carry-in (unchanged), but it must not STAY on the wrong project.
2. Repeat step 1 several times across a normal working session over the following days. **Expect:** the false "a newer version was saved on another device" banner does not appear from this browsing pattern. If it does appear, check whether a second real device/tab was open at the same time (a genuine conflict, unrelated to this fix) before treating it as a recurrence.
3. If a wrong-grid or false-banner report ever recurs, check Supabase `client_errors` for a `schedule-route-grid-divergence` event around that time (module `scheduler`) — its continued absence would point away from this exact mechanism and toward something new, rather than a re-litigation of this fix.
**Result:** ⏳ pending.

### V314448 — B623728: food map basemap + clustering, on his own signed-in account, real pin density `Blocker: real-data`
**⛔ ROUND 2, 2026-08-18/19 — this pass produced a REAL owner-visible defect that a code-only "sandbox proves it clean" check had missed, and it was caught by a colleague's own live check, not by this branch re-reading its own code.** The colleague loaded `planyr.io/#/food` directly and reported: basemap colour and the 1-10 rating scale are correct (confirmed, taken on his authority); but at Leaflet zoom 12 — the default, whole-metro view, the exact one the owner screenshotted and rejected twice — the map still drew 1,000 unrated reference pins with a "Showing 1,000 of 9,697 here" pill, because `MIN_PIN_ZOOM` (12) was identical to the default zoom and the "only his own places" rule never actually engaged there. **Round 1's sandbox pass below was a real, honest check of what it checked — it just never checked the one thing that mattered, because nothing in this sandbox can render a zoom level's worth of pins without reaching the blocked hosts.**
**What was verified this round, and the honest boundary of it.** `MIN_PIN_ZOOM` raised 12→15, chosen by three independent measurements run directly against production and Houston's own geometry (ground-scale meters-per-pixel, miles-across-at-1440px, and the decisive test — at z15 even the metro's single densest cluster, downtown/midtown at 1,251 places, stays under the reference-snapshot RPC's 2,000-row cap, while the same box at z14 already exceeds it at 2,641) — full numbers on B623728/BACKLOG.md. `npx vitest run` 87/87 green including a new recurrence guard pinning `MIN_PIN_ZOOM === 15` so a regression back toward 12-13 fails the build outright. **What this round could NOT do, stated plainly rather than blurred into the above:** load `#/food` in an actual browser and watch it render. This sandbox's egress proxy returned a confirmed POLICY DENIAL (403 on the CONNECT, logged by the proxy's own `/__agentproxy/status`, not a timeout) for both `basemaps.cartocdn.com` and `*.supabase.co` when re-tried this round via both `curl` and a real headless-Chromium `page.goto`, which itself hit `ERR_CONNECTION_RESET` on `planyr.io/#/food` even though the bare domain answers 200. So the corrected threshold's actual on-screen behaviour — pin count, banner text, the reference pins' visual weight — is reconstructed from direct SQL measurement of what the app's own query would return at each zoom, not watched.
**Why this needs his machine, restated for round 2:** the exact thing the colleague's report caught — what actually renders at a given zoom — is precisely what this sandbox cannot produce, for the two hosts this feature depends on. ### V304880 — B550512: exported PDF/PNG aerial imagery looks measurably sharper on a large site, on his own signed-in plan `Blocker: real-data` `Blocker: live-GIS`
**What was verified here (sandbox, real DOM code — `fetchTileImage` / `fetchTileImageByDeadline` / `stitchAerialDataUrl`, mirrored verbatim from `exportSheet.js` — driven end to end in real headless Chromium against a local HTTP/2 mock CDN with the same CORS shape and tile-URL scheme Esri/USGS use; five scenarios, `ui-audit/verify-aerial-tile-stitch.mjs`, all green, three consecutive clean runs):** a 300ft frame (already at Esri's native zoom ceiling) engages the sharpen pass ZERO times — byte-identical output, ~90-100ms; a 3,200ft frame with the deeper tiles arriving in time jumps from a 1882×1882px source stitch to 3764×3764px (**2.00× linear resolution**) in ~1.3-1.9s; the same frame with every deeper tile deliberately slow (3s each) falls back cleanly to the base 1882×1882px result in ~1.05-1.1s, nowhere near the tiles' own 3s — the "never stalls past budget" guarantee, measured, not assumed; a mixed fast/slow batch produces a genuinely mixed-resolution composite (both the base and the sharper tile's colours present in the output) and still returns in ~1.3s; a failing BASE tile still returns null exactly as before B550512 (the B840 fallback chain is untouched). Full unit suite 11,535 green (13 new `deepenZoomFor` cases), lint 0, build green, bundle measured against a clean-tree baseline with no new breach.
**Why this needs his machine, not just this sandbox:** the sandbox's headless browser cannot reach `server.arcgisonline.com` at all — a TLS-inspecting proxy resets the tunnel before the TLS handshake completes — so nothing here can measure the REAL Esri CDN's latency, HTTP/2 concurrent-stream ceiling, or the actual sharpness gain on a real printed sheet. And the gain only shows on a site whose printed frame is wide enough to have crossed the ~2,500ft threshold where the base stitch already backs off from Esri's sharpest zoom — a small site (under roughly 100 acres square) is already at the ceiling and will look and time IDENTICAL to before, which is correct, not a bug.

Compare the aerial imagery on the new PDF/PNG against one exported before this change (or against the on-screen zoomed-in view). **Expected: the satellite photo reads noticeably less blurred/upscaled** — buildings, driveways and lot lines on the imagery should look crisper, closer to (but likely still short of) the sharpness of the drawn vectors (buildings, parcels, text), which were always crisp.

5. Try it with a flaky or throttled connection if convenient (or just note the case): **Expected: the export still finishes promptly and never hangs waiting on the aerial** — worst case it looks the same as it did before this shipped, never worse and never stalled.
6. Confirm the existing "couldn't load the satellite imagery" banner (B735/B840) still only appears on a genuine full failure, not on the sharpen pass alone declining to complete — a sharpen miss is silent by design (LOUD-FAILURE only covers the aerial being dropped entirely, not this optional quality pass falling back to the same picture the export already produced before).

### V193168 — B391072 (×3): a purge is still gone HOURS later, with another window in play `Blocker: auth`

⛔ **This one has been reported fixed twice and was not.** His instruction, verbatim: *"Do not close this on another same-session test."* Proven without a browser at the layer where it is decided — `test/notesBinPurge.test.js` answers all four of his acceptance conditions as four named tests, including six adopt cycles against a server that keeps being handed a pre-purge tree — but the thing that failed last time was a path nobody exercised, so the account is the last mile.

- **PURGE SOMETHING, THEN COME BACK HOURS LATER.** PASS = the id is absent from the live list AND the bin, locally and in the cloud, on a re-look **hours** after the purge — not minutes, not the same session.
- **WITH ANOTHER WINDOW IN PLAY.** Leave a second window open that has not seen the purge. PASS = it does not put the page back, and the cloud's live page count does not go up.
- **⛔ AND NOTHING WITH A PURGED BODY MAY RENDER AS A NOTE.** PASS = no note in the sidebar opens empty with nothing recoverable behind it. That is the shape this recurrence took.
- **AN ORDINARY DELETE STILL WORKS.** Bin a note; it is still restorable. A tombstone buries a PURGE, never a delete.
- **A NULL IS NOT A DISPOSITION (STANDING RULE #2).** Reported fixed twice already — if it cannot be provoked, say so and take one of the three admissible routes, naming which.
**✅ PASSED — verified on the owner's own signed-in account, 2026-08-13.** He ran the two-window case
this sandbox cannot reach, and it holds in the STRONGER form: the purge did not merely survive, it
PROPAGATED. Window B created `TWOWIN` (`pg_msqzi8nj1mghpu8`); window A reloaded, saw it, binned it and
deleted it forever; window B — still holding `TWOWIN` in its own view at a PRE-PURGE revision — was
then forced to write and push by creating a new page in it. `TWOWIN` did not come back: not in window
B, not in local storage, not in the cloud (**tree rev 1307, `twowin_back` false**). **Window B had
already dropped it from its own list before the forced write**, which is the propagation rather than
the mere survival. Single-window purge also held across two reloads, twice, local and cloud. His
baseline is restored exactly: **10 live · bin 24 · `live_but_purged` 0.** This closes the item that
broke three times — B357011 shipped the rule, B364016 found `migrate` wiping the ledger, B391072
found it running on only one of the two adopt paths.

### V165104 — B369536: on or after **2026-09-18**, does the retention job actually DELETE? `Blocker: real-data`

**Due 2026-09-19, and the extra day is not slack — read this before filing a failure.** The oldest row is **2026-06-20 22:16:28 UTC**, so it crosses 90 days at **2026-09-18 22:16 UTC** — *after* that morning's 07:20 run. **The first run that can delete anything is 2026-09-19 07:20 UTC.** A read on 2026-09-18 will correctly return `WAIT` and proves nothing; do not report that as a failure. A one-shot Routine is armed for **2026-09-19 08:00 UTC**; if it is not honoured, run it by hand.

**⛔ THE ONE THING THAT CAN RUIN THIS CHECK, AND IT TAKES ONE KEYSTROKE: do NOT call `select public.prune_client_errors()`.** A hand-run writes a run row byte-identical to a scheduled one, so it manufactures exactly the evidence this check exists to gather, permanently and undetectably. That is the same trap V84560 was written around, and it is why the reader below is `select`-only. Do not seed rows, do not age a row "to test it", do not help it along.

**Steps.** Paste **QUERY 1** from `src/shared/telemetry/client_errors_retention_check.sql` into the Supabase SQL editor on `lyeqzkuiwngunutlkkmi`. One row comes back. Then paste **QUERY 2** from the bottom of the same file (commented out) for the independent pg_cron corroboration.

**Expect / PASS** = `verdict` reads **`PASS-first-deletion-observed`**, with `ordinary_missed 0`, `manual_missed 0`, a non-null `first_deletion_run_id`, and `liveness = ok`. QUERY 2 shows one `succeeded` cron row per calendar day, each paired with exactly one run row.

**FAIL, and they mean different things:**
- **`FAIL-policy-not-applied`** — the job fired, reported success, and left rows behind that were past 90 days when it ran. **The policy is broken, not the check.** Re-open B369536 with a `Recurrence:` line; the number to report is `ordinary_missed`.
- **`FAIL-stale`** / **`FAIL-never-run`** — the schedule has stopped. This is a B270913 recurrence (its stopping rule named exactly this), not a new item.
- **`WAIT-no-eligible-rows-yet` after 2026-09-19** — not a pass and not a "check again later". The 2026-09-18 date is derived from the oldest row (2026-06-20 22:16:28 + 90 days); if nothing was eligible, either that row was removed by something else or the arithmetic is wrong. Re-open and say which.
- **A `succeeded` cron row in QUERY 2 with NO run row beside it** — worse than any of the above: the function ran and its unconditional insert did not land. That is a new defect, not this one.

**What is already proven, so this is a confirmation and not a discovery.** `test/clientErrorsRetentionCheck.test.js` (26) runs the shipped `.sql` files verbatim against a real Postgres and produces all five verdicts from seeded data at a fast-forwarded clock — including the first deletion, the manual capture surviving beside it, and the `FAIL-policy-not-applied` case mutation-proven by widening the shipped 90-day window to 400. The reader is proven read-only against a live database, and proven unable to be satisfied by an off-schedule (hand) run. It was executed against **production** on 2026-08-11 and returned `WAIT-no-eligible-rows-yet` · 3 scheduled runs · 1 off-schedule · 5,707 rows · next eligible **2026-09-18** — so the query itself is known to work there; only the date is owed.

**A NULL IS NOT A DISPOSITION (STANDING RULE #2).** Whatever comes back, record it here with the date and archive per rule 3. Do not close this on "nothing to see yet".

### V107264 — B296224: the ledger bridge resolves a REAL `dirty` PR, and refuses a REAL amendment race `Blocker: real-data`

**Everything the bridge decides is proven here already** — `test/resolveLedgers.test.js` drives 12 cases, three of them against a genuine `git merge` conflict produced in a throwaway repo (hermetic, no network): two independent appends are unioned, two amendments of one item are refused with the markers left in place, and a clean file passes through byte-identical. **What a sandbox cannot manufacture is the real thing**: this repo's actual `origin/main`, 42 in-flight branches, five bookkeeping files diverging at once, and the specific hunk shapes git produces from them. That is a concurrency class, so it parks.

- **NEXT TIME A PR HERE GOES `mergeable_state: dirty`** — which on this repo's traffic is a matter of hours — resolve it with `git fetch origin main && git merge origin/main` and then `npm run resolve-ledgers` **instead of editing the conflict markers by hand.**
- **PASS** = it reports the files and hunk counts it unioned, `git status` shows them staged, the conflict markers are gone, `BACKLOG_OPEN.md` and `MAP.md` were regenerated rather than concatenated, and `npm test` is green afterwards (in particular `idUniqueness`, `ledgerDuplicateIds` and `backlogIndex`).
- **ALSO A PASS, and the more valuable outcome:** it REFUSES, names an id that appears on both sides, and writes nothing. That is the amendment race the bridge exists to stop a union from silently duplicating — record which id, and that the markers were still intact for the hand merge.
- **FAIL** = it resolves a hunk where the same id really was on both sides, leaves a conflict marker behind, stages a file it did not fully resolve, or reports success while `npm test` then goes red.
- **Record either way in `.planyr-ledger-merges.log`'s terms** (`resolved` / `refused` / `rolled-back`): that tally is the evidence deciding whether option (c) — the ~1,400-item migration — is worth doing. **If `refused` never fires across a month of merges, the conflicts are 100% arrival-order and (c) is justified by data.** If it fires often, the bridge is already doing the important half and (c) is less urgent than it looks.
- **✅ PASS — 2026-08-09, PR #989 (`resolved`).** The PR went `mergeable_state: dirty` within a minute of being opened (which is why its `build` check was never created — GitHub cannot build a test-merge ref that does not exist). `git fetch origin main && git merge origin/main` produced conflicts in **`BACKLOG.md`, `BACKLOG_OPEN.md` and `VERIFICATION.md`**; `npm run resolve-ledgers` unioned **2 files / 2 hunks** with no id on both sides, **regenerated `BACKLOG_OPEN.md`** rather than concatenating it, staged them, and left zero conflict markers. `MAP.md` and `BACKLOG_OPEN.md` drift checks passed and the full suite was green afterwards (511 files / 10,268 tests, `idUniqueness` and `backlogIndex` among them). Logged `{"outcome":"resolved","files":2,"hunks":2}`. **The `refused` branch did not fire** — one more data point for the option-(c) tally.

3. **The ETJ dedupe hid the ETJ on split sites.** Dropping an ETJ whose city already holds the site is right when it holds ALL of it and wrong when it holds part — the case that needs it most.

**The coverage hole, measured (B280705):** the H-GAC "regional" ETJ layer carries **34 cities**; Baytown, Katy, Humble, La Porte, Deer Park, Friendswood, League City, Galveston and Tomball are not among them. ### V665 — B1346 (the REFUTED two-renders-per-pan claim: confirm on the owner's own heavy plan that there is genuinely no second commit). `Blocker: real-data` — a refutation measured on a light scene is the weakest kind, and this one closes an item rather than opening one, so it deserves the real check. On **planyr.io**, signed in, open the heaviest real plan and confirm — **(a) WITH THE REACT PROFILER:** record a few seconds of panning in the React DevTools Profiler and count committed renders against painted frames. One commit per pointermove is the expected reading; two would re-open **B1346**. **(b) THE COORDINATE READOUT:** while panning, watch the latitude/longitude readout — it must keep up with the pointer, not lag it by a frame. If it ever lags, the cursor commit has fallen out of the pan's batch and the claim becomes true again. **(c) THE REGISTRATION:** with the aerial on, pan hard and confirm the drawing stays welded to the imagery (B1122) — the registration effect was measured here as costing ONE extra commit across a whole gesture, and a real plan should not change that. ⏳ **LIVE APP (planyr.io), SIGNED IN, ON REAL PROJECT DATA** `Blocker: real-data`
- **Verified in-session 2026-07-31 (the measurement that refuted it — DRIVEN, not reasoned).** `ui-audit/diagnose-pan-commits.mjs`, new: **1.02–1.10 DOM-commit batches per pointermove event** (60 events → 1.10 · 120 → 1.05 · 240 → 1.02). Of 62 batches touching the coordinate readout, **61 were batched WITH the pan commit** and exactly **1** stood alone; the registration effect accounted for **1** batch across the whole gesture. The apparent 2× in the first pass was the measuring driver's own artefact (`mouse.move(..., {steps: 2})` dispatches two events per call) and is written into the source so it cannot be reintroduced. **No fix shipped** — there is no phantom to fix.
- **What the sandbox CANNOT prove, and why this stays `live`:** React's batching depends on scheduler timing, and on a machine slow enough for a render to overrun the frame the rAF cursor job could land in the NEXT frame's commit instead of this one's. That is exactly the owner's machine on the owner's plan.

### V538 — B1158 (gating the stormwater derivation changed WHEN it runs and nothing about WHAT it says): on **planyr.io**, signed in, on a real project with a drawn pond and a checked drainage screen (Tsakiris / Bain), confirm — **(a) THE NUMBERS ARE IDENTICAL:** open Yield → Stormwater and compare every figure against what it read before this shipped — required vs provided detention, the mitigation ledger, drawdown, the storage reconciliation, the administrator row, the apron check, the cut/fill balance. ### V539 — B1160 (releasing canvas backing stores actually moves the owner's 555 MB) — **STILL OPEN, and confirmed unanswerable from here (B1357, 2026-07-31).** `performance.measureUserAgentSpecificMemory()` requires cross-origin isolation, which the app does not set, so it is unavailable in this sandbox AND on planyr.io; and the long-session harness decoded zero tiles, so the sustained-panning half could not be exercised either. This is production-only, exactly as filed. Original terms follow: on **planyr.io**, with Chrome's **Task Manager** open (Window → Task Manager — it reports per-tab memory, which a JS heap snapshot cannot see), confirm — **(a) THE MEASUREMENT THAT MOTIVATED THIS:** open a large PDF in Review and pan continuously for 60 seconds; note the tab's Memory Footprint before and after, and compare against the same run on the previous release. The detail raster re-renders on a 140 ms throttle throughout, so this is the single biggest producer of offscreen canvases in the app; **(b) THE BREAKDOWN:** in the console, run `await performance.measureUserAgentSpecificMemory()` and read the `Canvas` type specifically — that is the allocator this item is aimed at, and the number that should have moved; **(c) THE PDF OVERLAY:** in the Site Planner, drop a large PDF site plan as a reference and zoom in and out repeatedly across the re-raster bands (each pass allocates up to an 8192-wide RGBA buffer, roughly 180 MB), and confirm memory returns rather than stepping up per zoom; **(d) NOTHING LOOKS WORSE — this is the risk, and it is the point of a live pass:** the Review page never flashes blank or shows a stale tile while panning; a re-rastered PDF overlay is as sharp as before; the mitigation heat-map still paints; **(e) OCR:** run the auto-filing OCR path on a scanned sheet and confirm it still reads the title block — its canvas is released by the OCR runner in a `finally`, so a failure there would show as OCR returning nothing; **(f) A LONG SESSION:** work normally for 20–30 minutes across Site and Review and confirm the tab's footprint plateaus rather than climbing. ⏳ **LIVE APP (planyr.io) — Chrome Task Manager on a real session with a real PDF** `Blocker: real-data` *(implemented + verified as far as this sandbox can reach, 2026-07-30. **ATTEMPT-BEFORE-YOU-PARK honoured:** every release site is unit-guarded — `test/renderBudgetMemos.test.js` asserts the helper zeroes both dimensions, is a no-op on nullish and never throws on a hostile object, that the two per-workspace copies have not drifted, and, per file, that the release fires AFTER the call that takes the pixels out and never before; plus that the OCR raster is released by its OWNER and not by the module that rendered it. Full suite green, build green, bundle budgets within ceiling. **Why it cannot go further here:** `performance.measureUserAgentSpecificMemory()` needs cross-origin isolation, which the app does not set, so full-tab memory is not measurable from a script at all — and Chrome's Task Manager is a human reading a real window. This is a memory item whose whole claim is a number only a real session can produce.)* *(minted V539 alongside B1160; references **B1160**; related to **B1121** (tile memory — the other allocator, already capped) and **B1063** (the standing tile-request breach); `Cadence: once`)*

### V386 — B914: a loose PDF last-opened in one project no longer leaks its "upload didn't finish" banner onto every OTHER project's Review tab; each project's Review reopens ITS own last drawing (or a clean empty state), and Open works ⏳ **LIVE APP (planyr.io), SIGNED IN — at least two projects, one WITHOUT its own last drawing (Mesa / a scratch project)** (cross-project resume + real signed-in project data — the leak needs a real orphaned review in the cloud)  *(minted V386 via `npm run next-id`; references **B914**; branch `claude/v331-v332-v333-verification-iqgthn`; `Cadence: once`)*
- **Pending live steps (signed in):** (1) With a large loose PDF as the most-recently-opened drawing anywhere, go to the Review tab of a project that has never had a drawing (Mesa, or a fresh scratch project) → it shows the clean **"No drawing open"** empty state, NOT the other project's file name in the Reviews field and NOT its "…cloud upload didn't finish…" banner. (2) Click **Open PDF…** and pick a PDF → it opens normally (the stuck orphan no longer swallows the Open). (3) A project that DOES remember its own last drawing still reopens THAT drawing on return. (4) Empty-state hint sanity: open **⇄ Compare revisions…** and cancel the picker → no "Pick exactly two PDFs…" error is left stuck; switch projects → the hint never carries over.
- **Verified here (sandbox/headless, 2026-07-21):** the fix is a pure guard — `resumeAllowedForRoute(routeProjectId, recProjectId)` in `lib/lastDoc.js`, unit-tested for the exact leak matrix (no route → allow anything; named route → exact match only; named route BLOCKS a null/undefined-projectId orphan), 17 `lastDoc` tests green. Logged-out headless smoke of `#/markup`: the Review empty state renders "No drawing open" + the three buttons, **no** phantom "Pick exactly two PDFs" hint, **no** stuck banner, 0 page errors. Full suite + lint 0 + build green; `MAP.md` regenerated.
- **Blocker: real-data** — reproducing the actual cross-project leak needs a real orphaned (unfiled, upload-incomplete) review in the signed-in account plus ≥2 real projects; the sandbox egress CORS-blocks Supabase sign-in, so `loadReview` can't run logged-out. The pure decision is fully unit-proven above; only the end-to-end "banner no longer appears on Mesa/ZZ" needs a signed-in browser.
- **⏳ ROUND-2 diagnosis + fix (2026-07-21, Cowork live re-test on Mesa + this session's code fix):** the leak STILL reproduced live — Mesa's Review tab showed the "Goose Creek PI APPROVED PLANS — BC25010002.pdf" banner/Reviews-field name even though the network fetch resolved to Mesa's OWN doc (`id=eq.rvmqoihur10mmbv`, server title "Mesa - Civil - 2023.03.06"). So PR #729's `resumeAllowedForRoute` HELPER is correct, but it was being **called with the boot-resume effect's mount-time `projectId` closure**. Root cause: `DocReview.jsx`'s resume effect has `[]` deps, so on a deep link — where the `projectId` prop lands a beat AFTER mount — the effect's captured route is still null while a slow legacy-global orphan's `loadReview()` is in flight; the guard `resumeAllowedForRoute(null, …)` waved the projectId-less orphan through, and because its await finished LAST it superseded the correct per-project doc the project-switch effect had already opened. **Fix (this session):** the resume loop now guards on a live `routeIdRef.current` (a ref mirroring the `projectId` prop every render) instead of the stale closure, AND stands down (`return`) if `openInFlightRef.current` shows a route-driven open already owns the outcome. Full suite (4748) + lint 0 + build green; the fix is a React effect-timing race so it can't boot headless (doc-review needs signed-in real data).
- **Still ⏳ live:** the round-2 fix is reasoned + build/test-green but the actual "banner no longer appears on Mesa when deep-linked with a loose orphan last-opened globally" needs one signed-in cross-project click-through (Blocker: real-data, as above).
- On pass: move B914 from ⏳ Verify → BACKLOG-DONE, and this entry → VERIFICATION-DONE.
